<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Many biological discovery problems require experiments to be selected sequentially under constrained budgets. CRISPR screening is a prominent example, as exhaustive perturbation testing is often infeasible and candidate perturbations must instead be prioritized over multiple experimental rounds. Despite the importance of this problem, existing benchmarks for adaptive hit discovery remain limited in scale and diversity.
Here, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span>, a large-scale benchmark for adaptive hit discovery comprising 1,389 CRISPR screens across five phenotype categories. Beyond enabling systematic evaluation, its scale makes it possible to learn acquisition strategies across historical experiments.
Building on this resource, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span>, a sequential experimental design framework combining <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>, a transformer-based amortized acquisition policy trained across historical screens to adapt from experimental feedback, with LLM-derived biological priors through an adaptive handoff. In this view, completed experiments become training data for learning how accumulated evidence should guide what to test next, while LLMs provide prior biological knowledge to seed the search. We further introduce <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span>, showing that the same principle can be extended directly to an LLM through task-specific post-training.
On temporally held-out screens, <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> achieves a 5.67-fold enrichment over random selection and recovers 27.7% of hits after assaying approximately 5% of the candidate library, outperforming existing adaptive-design methods and standalone LLMs, and <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> alone. Performance improves with increasing historical training data and transfers to phenotype categories excluded from training.
These results demonstrate the value of learning acquisition policies across historical experiments and combining them with broad biological priors for efficient adaptive hit discovery.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><a href="https://genentech.github.io/AssayLoop" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href" style="font-size:120%;">

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CRISPR screens are central tools in functional genomics and drug discovery, enabling systematic perturbation of gene function and measurement of heterogeneous phenotypic effects <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>. Yet the space of possible perturbations is vast, spanning thousands of genes across diverse cellular contexts, disease models, and phenotypic readouts. Exhaustive experimentation is therefore often infeasible, particularly when the biological question requires richer models or phenotypes that cannot be measured in highly multiplexed formats. In these settings, only a fraction of candidate perturbations can be tested, often over a sequence of experimental rounds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.
Efficient screen design, selecting the most informative experiments to perform next, is therefore essential for rapidly identifying biologically meaningful effects.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Sequential experimental design provides a natural framework for this setting: a model proposes experiments, observes their outcomes, and uses this feedback to determine subsequent actions under a finite budget <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. This model-experiment interaction forms a lab-in-the-loop process, in which experimental outcomes guide the next round of decisions. Closing this loop is a core capability for emerging AI-driven and increasingly autonomous scientific systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Several methods have applied this principle to perturbation-screen design. DiscoBAX proposed an objective-driven Bayesian active-learning method encouraging coverage of diverse biological mechanisms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>. BioBO incorporates multimodal gene representations and pathway information into Bayesian optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>. Probability-of-Hit fits a probabilistic surrogate to observations collected from the current screen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>. However, these approaches treat each new experiment largely as an independent problem, fitting predictive models or acquisition strategies for each new screen. Therefore, while they can adapt to assay-specific feedback, they do not leverage the growing collection of related experiments that have already been completed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) have recently been explored as an alternative, serving as acquisition policies for biological experimental design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>. By conditioning on natural-language descriptions of the experimental setting, LLMs can draw on broad scientific knowledge to prioritize plausible candidates before any observation has been collected. However, whether LLMs reliably adapt their acquisition strategies from experimental feedback remains an open question, with recent studies reaching conflicting conclusions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>. This reveals a central tension in adaptive biological experimentation: effective acquisition requires both strong prior knowledge for initial prioritization and a reliable mechanism for learning from assay-specific observations as they accumulate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the importance of adaptive hit discovery for functional genomics and target identification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, existing benchmarks remain limited in scale and diversity. GeneDisco introduced evaluation protocols for active-learning policies on genetic perturbation experiments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, but contains only four immunology-focused screens, and other studies have evaluated sequential design on similarly narrow collections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>. No general-purpose, multi-phenotype benchmark at a scale that would support both rigorous evaluation and the training of transferable acquisition policies has been available. Such a resource is necessary not only to evaluate sequential-design methods, but to ask a broader question: can experimental systems learn from experience accumulated across many previous experiments?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we address both the benchmarking gap and the methodological tension outlined above (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). First, we introduce <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span>, a large-scale benchmark for adaptive hit discovery comprising 1,389 CRISPR screens across five phenotype categories, equipped with dedicated metrics that account for hit-rate heterogeneity and incomplete ground truth. Beyond enabling systematic evaluation, the scale of <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> makes it possible to learn acquisition strategies from historical experiments rather than fitting each screen independently.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Building on this resource, we introduce <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span>, a sequential experimental design framework that combines an amortized acquisition policy trained across historical screens with biological prior knowledge derived from an LLM. At its core is <span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>, a transformer-based policy that learns, across historical assays, how experimental feedback should modify candidate prioritization, and transfers these learned strategies to new assays at inference time. In this view, completed experiments become training data for learning how to experiment, i.e., how evidence accumulated during a new campaign should guide what to test next. <span id="S1.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> complements this learned policy with LLM-derived biological priors through an adaptive handoff: an LLM guides early acquisitions when assay-specific evidence is limited, before transitioning to <span id="S1.p7.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> as experimental observations accumulate. This design combines two complementary capabilities: broad biological prior knowledge for early prioritization, and a feedback-conditioned policy learned from historical experiments for subsequent adaptation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We further explore whether the same principle, learning adaptive acquisition behavior from historical screens, can be realized directly within an LLM through task-specific post-training. To this end, we introduce <span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span>, a 27B-parameter LLM fine-tuned on acquisition trajectories and subsequently optimized with reinforcement learning over sequential campaigns, providing a proof of principle for this strategy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">On temporally held-out screens, <span id="S1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> achieves a 5.67-fold enrichment over random selection and recovers 27.7% of hits after assaying only approximately 5% of the candidate library, outperforming existing adaptive-design methods, standalone LLMs, and its core policy used alone. We further show that the learned acquisition strategy transfers to unseen phenotype categories and improves with increasing amounts of historical training data, supporting the idea that experimental decision-making can be amortized across historical experiments. Across acquired perturbations, <span id="S1.p9.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> retains broad biological pathway coverage while improving hit discovery. Analysis of the learned acquisition policy further reveals directional gene-gene influence patterns, including relationships supported by prior biological evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these results establish historical experimental repositories as a substrate for evaluating and learning transferable decision-making.
By coupling learned policies with pretrained biological knowledge and accumulated experimental feedback, we provide a framework for improving sequential experimental design across new biological screens. More broadly, these findings suggest a path toward lab-in-the-loop systems that accumulate experimental experience across campaigns and use it to support increasingly autonomous, adaptive experimentation in biology.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>A large collection of historical CRISPR screens enables learning a transferable acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formalize adaptive hit discovery as a sequential experimental design problem (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 A large collection of historical CRISPR screens enables learning a transferable acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>A). A CRISPR screen <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is defined by a natural-language description <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> of the experimental setup, a screen library <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> of the genes measured in that screen, and binary hit labels <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{g}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{g}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> for each <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g\in L_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g\in L_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Because a single policy must act across screens with different libraries, we additionally define a fixed candidate gene pool <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, shared by all screens and containing every screen library (<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{s}\subseteq\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>⊆</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{s}\subseteq\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At each round <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}</annotation></semantics></math>, the model selects a batch <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> genes, observes their hit labels, and accumulates a history <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. The goal is to maximize the total number of discovered hits within the fixed budget <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\times b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\times b</annotation></semantics></math> by learning an acquisition policy <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi(B_{t}\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi(B_{t}\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Asking whether completed experiments can inform future ones requires a collection of screens large enough to both train and evaluate acquisition strategies. To this end, we introduce <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span>, a large-scale compendium of historical CRISPR screens for adaptive hit discovery built upon AssayBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> comprises 1,389 CRISPR screens across five phenotype categories, with a temporal train/validation/test split (1,349/20/20 screens; Fig. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 A large collection of historical CRISPR screens enables learning a transferable acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>B).
Validation and test screens were restricted to genome-wide assays with sufficient hit signal and non-trivial baseline recoverability, and were then selected to provide broad phenotype coverage and maximize within-category diversity of screen descriptions (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 A large collection of historical CRISPR screens enables learning a transferable acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>C; selection details in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Dataset Composition ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, phenotype composition in Supplementary Table <a href="#A1.T1" title="Supplementary Table 1 ‣ Appendix A Dataset Composition ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and per-screen characteristics in Supplementary Table <a href="#A1.T2" title="Supplementary Table 2 ‣ Appendix A Dataset Composition ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Test screens are substantially different from the training set (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 A large collection of historical CRISPR screens enables learning a transferable acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>E; median test-to-training hit-set Jaccard similarity <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.064" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.064</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.064</annotation></semantics></math>). At the same time, <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> spans a broad hit repertoire: although the most recurrent hits are enriched for DepMap common-essential genes, many non-essential genes also recur as hits across multiple screens (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 A large collection of historical CRISPR screens enables learning a transferable acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>F). This structure motivates acquisition policies that can exploit recurrent cross-screen structure while retaining broad coverage of the gene space, rather than collapsing onto a small set of ubiquitous hits.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/Figure2_Framework_revised.svg" id="S2.SS1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/342;" width="476" height="342"></object>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Figure 2: <span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop<span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> is a large-scale compendium and benchmark for adaptive hit discovery in CRISPR screens.</span></span>
<span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>, Problem setup. An acquisition policy receives a natural-language description <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> of
the screen (cell line, perturbation modality, treatment and readout) and, over <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rounds,
nominates a batch <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> genes to perturb, observes their binary hit labels, and conditions
the next batch on the accumulated history. The objective is to maximize the number of hits
discovered within the fixed budget <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\times b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\times b</annotation></semantics></math> (here <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=10</annotation></semantics></math> rounds of <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b=100</annotation></semantics></math> genes, i.e. 1,000
acquisitions per screen).
<span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">B</span>, Benchmark construction. Starting from <span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, screen
prompts were adapted to the sequential setting and the temporally held-out validation (2021) and
test (<math id="S2.SS1.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>2021) pools were filtered to 20 genome-wide screens each.
The resulting <span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> comprises 1,389 screens split temporally into 1,349 training,
20 validation and 20 test screens.
<span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">C</span>, Phenotype composition of each split across the five phenotype categories. Training
screens are dominated by fitness/proliferation assays, whereas validation and test screens were
selected to spread across categories and to maximize within-category diversity of screen
descriptions.
<span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">D</span>, Evaluation. Metrics are defined over the candidate gene pool <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, the screen
library <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>, the hit set <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> and the acquired genes <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math>. The primary metric is the hit enrichment
factor (EF), defined as the ratio of hits found to the number expected under random selection. The normalization penalizes hallucinated and unfilled acquisitions but does not penalize valid genes absent from the retrospective screen library. Secondary metrics include the normalized area under the
cumulative-hits curve (nAUC), the fraction of hits found (FH), and the effective number of Reactome
pathway groups (EP). <span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">E</span>, Jaccard similarity between the hit set in each screen and the nearest training screen. The histogram separates within-training screens from the same or different publications; points show validation and test screens, and dashed lines mark the train-train and test medians. <span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">F</span>, Training hit frequency by gene (green; symlog scale) and the fraction of DepMap common-essential genes in a 201-gene rolling window (orange). <span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">G</span>, Hit-rate distribution across all 1,389 screens, with validation and test screens below (each point is a screen); the dashed line marks the median.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluating adaptive hit discovery requires metrics that account for substantial variation in baseline screen difficulty (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 A large collection of historical CRISPR screens enables learning a transferable acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>G) and incomplete retrospective ground truth. Not all genes in <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> are measured in every screen, and LLM-based policies can hallucinate invalid gene names or return incomplete batches. To this end, our primary metric is the hit enrichment factor (EF), defined as the ratio of discovered hits to the expected number under random selection, with a normalization that penalizes hallucinated genes but not valid genes absent from the screen library (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 A large collection of historical CRISPR screens enables learning a transferable acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>D; Methods). We additionally report the normalized area under the cumulative-hits curve (nAUC), the fraction of hits found (FH), and the effective number of Reactome pathway groups (EP) as a measure of biological diversity (eight metrics in total; Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Metrics used in AssayBench-Loop ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>). All results are reported at a fixed acquisition budget per screen (10 rounds of 100 requested genes).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> provides a substantially larger historical training resource than existing benchmarks, while its held-out evaluation sets comprise phenotype-diverse genome-wide screens. For example, GeneDisco <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> is two orders of magnitude smaller, spanning four immunology screens, and other evaluations have used similarly narrow collections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>. <span id="S2.SS1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> provides the scale to learn a transferable acquisition strategy from historical experiments, rather than fitting each screen independently, motivating the amortized approach we describe next.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span><span id="S2.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> learns a feedback-conditioned acquisition policy across experiments, which <span id="S2.SS2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> combines with LLM priors</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing sequential design methods for CRISPR screens fit a separate surrogate model for each new experiment and do not transfer acquisition strategies across screens. In contrast, we learn a shared, history-conditioned acquisition policy across all historical screens, following the amortized experimental design paradigm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>. Here, the policy itself is amortized, meaning that a single set of parameters maps any screen description and accumulated experimental history to a ranking over candidate genes. Thus, the strategy for translating experimental feedback into the next action is learned from a large collection of completed experiments. The resulting policy transfers the learned screening strategy to new assays at inference time while adapting its decisions based on the perturbation-outcome pairs observed during the current experiment (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 AssayFormer learns a feedback-conditioned acquisition policy across experiments, which AssayLoop combines with LLM priors ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>A).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We instantiate this policy as a transformer encoder, <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>, that takes as input the screen description <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> and the history of observed gene–outcome pairs <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, and produces acquisition scores over all candidate genes (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 AssayFormer learns a feedback-conditioned acquisition policy across experiments, which AssayLoop combines with LLM priors ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>B, Methods). Each observed gene is represented by a learnable embedding combined with a learned hit-indicator token. The screen description is encoded through a frozen text encoder and projected into the transformer’s latent space. The transformer jointly processes the sequence of observed genes with the description token, and the output embedding at the description position is scored against all candidate gene embeddings via a bilinear head to obtain per-gene acquisition scores. At inference time, batches are selected greedily according to these scores. Full architectural details are provided in Methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Training proceeds in three stages (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 AssayFormer learns a feedback-conditioned acquisition policy across experiments, which AssayLoop combines with LLM priors ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>C, Methods). First, gene embeddings are initialized using Bayesian Probabilistic Matrix Factorization (BPMF) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> on the binary hit matrix across training screens, thereby capturing cross-screen co-hit structure. Second, the model is trained with supervised learning to predict hit labels for unobserved genes using binary cross-entropy. To mimic intermediate states of a sequential screen, we randomly sample observed gene sets of varying sizes during training. Third, the policy is fine-tuned with reinforcement learning using group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> on full <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>-step trajectory rollouts. Notably, a context-delta reward encourages the policy to leverage the experimentally revealed history by rewarding improvements over a context-free baseline (Methods).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> is explicitly trained to use experimental feedback, but its initial acquisitions rely primarily on cross-screen structure and the limited assay-specific information contained in the screen description.
We therefore combine the learned policy with LLM-derived biological priors through an adaptive handoff strategy (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 AssayFormer learns a feedback-conditioned acquisition policy across experiments, which AssayLoop combines with LLM priors ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>D).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para"><img src="2609.11877v1/Figure3_AssayFormer_revised.png" id="S2.SS2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:476/610;" width="476" height="610" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Figure 3: <span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">
<span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> combines <span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>, an amortized acquisition policy for adaptive hit discovery, with LLM prior knowledge.</span>
<span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>, Paradigms for active hit discovery. Conventional adaptive designs fit a surrogate model
independently for each new screen and do not transfer acquisition strategies across experiments.
LLM-based policies can exploit broad biological knowledge from the scientific literature, but are not explicitly trained across historical screens for feedback-conditioned adaptation. In contrast, <span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> follows an amortized design paradigm: it learns a shared,
history-conditioned acquisition policy across historical screens and combines it with LLM-derived priors.
<span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">B</span>, <span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> architecture. The screen description <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> is embedded by a frozen text
encoder and projected into the model’s latent space, while each previously assayed gene is represented by
a learnable gene token combined with a learned hit-indicator token. A transformer encoder
processes this unordered sequence, and the output embedding at the description position is scored against all
candidate gene embeddings through a bilinear head to produce per-gene acquisition scores
<math id="S2.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\phi}(g\mid h_{t-1},c_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\phi}(g\mid h_{t-1},c_{s})</annotation></semantics></math>. The next batch consists of the top-<math id="S2.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> previously untested genes.
<span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">C</span>, Three-stage training. Gene tokens are initialized by Bayesian probabilistic matrix
factorization (BPMF) of the binary hit matrix of the training screens.
The policy is then trained with binary cross-entropy (BCE) to predict hit labels for unobserved genes given simulated histories of varying length, and finally fine-tuned with GRPO on full <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>-step rollouts using a context-delta reward
that credits the policy only hits recovered beyond those obtained by a context-free reference policy.
<span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">D</span>, The <span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> handoff. An LLM acts as the acquisition policy for the first <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> rounds, providing a biologically informed warm start. <span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> then takes over for the remaining <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T-k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T-k</annotation></semantics></math> rounds and adapts to the accumulated experimental history. <span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">E</span>, Worked-out example of a genome-wide CRISPR screen for regulators of TNF<math id="S2.SS2.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>-induced NF-<math id="S2.SS2.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>B activity in HeLa cells (169 true hits). (Left) Ten-round AssayFormer trajectory. Proposed genes are above the axis and recovered hits below, colored by broad Reactome category; round 4 is highlighted. (Middle) Composition of the round-4 batch with labels withheld or available as context: both batches contain 100 genes and recover 7 or 11 hits, respectively. (Right) Ranks of the union of the top 20 genes with and without labels as context. Blue and orange indicate at least twofold promotion or demotion when labels are supplied, gray indicates smaller changes, green points mark true hits. Teal annotations show leave-one-label-out counterfactual ranks.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">For the first <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> rounds (<math id="S2.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=3</annotation></semantics></math>, selected on the validation set), which we refer to as the warm-start phase, an LLM serves as the acquisition policy, processing the screen description and accumulated history in context to propose biologically informed gene selections. <span id="S2.SS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> then hands off to <span id="S2.SS2.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> for the remaining <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T-k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T-k</annotation></semantics></math> rounds, allowing the learned policy to leverage the screen-specific feedback accumulated during the warm-start phase. This design combines two complementary capabilities: biological prior knowledge for early prioritization, provided by the LLM, and history-conditioned adaptation to subsequent experimental outcomes, learned by the trained policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In a representative genome-wide CRISPR screen for regulators of TNF<math id="S2.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>-induced NF-<math id="S2.SS2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>B activity, (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 AssayFormer learns a feedback-conditioned acquisition policy across experiments, which AssayLoop combines with LLM priors ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>E–G), <span id="S2.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> recovered 60 of 169 true hits within the first 1,000 assayed genes. At round 4, incorporating the 24 hit labels observed among the first 300 genes substantially reranked candidate genes for the next batch, producing a net increase from seven to eleven hits and expanding their represented pathways from four to nine categories. Leave-one-label-out counterfactuals further show that specific observations, such as KCTD10 and NHLRC2, contribute strongly to the prioritization of CYFIP1, YARS2, and STRAP (these dependencies describe the model’s decision process rather than established biological interactions).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span><span id="S2.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> improves adaptive hit discovery on held-out screens</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> was trained on the 1,349 historical screens in the <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench</span> training set and evaluated on the test set. A broad set of methods was also benchmarked in the same setting. These spanned adaptive experimental design algorithms, transfer learning, LLMs, and agentic approaches. Adaptive methods included Probability-of-Hit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> and BioBO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, which fit per-screen surrogates without leveraging historical data. Transfer-based baselines included BPMF with greedy acquisition, Screen-kNN (which scores candidates using hit rates from similar training screens), MAML <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> (which meta-learns an initialization across training screens that can be quickly adapted on the observed hit labels), and a prior-hit frequency baseline. We evaluated several LLM families (GLM, Kimi, Claude, Qwen, Gemini, GPT), spanning open- and closed-weight models at different sizes, and test each both with and without access to feedback labels. After each acquisition round, the accumulated experimental history is appended to the next prompt.
Finally, we included two agentic harnesses specifically designed for adaptive hit discovery, LLMNN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> and ICBR-EF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, and a general coding agent based on Claude Haiku-4.5 with direct access to the training screens. Full details of all tested methods are provided in Methods. Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.3 AssayLoop improves adaptive hit discovery on held-out screens ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes test set results, with full results reported in Supplementary Table <a href="#A3.T4" title="Supplementary Table 4 ‣ Appendix C Complete Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S2.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.T1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance comparison on held-out test screens<span id="S2.T1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. Metrics evaluate enrichment factor (EF; hit enrichment relative to random selection), normalized area under the cumulative-hits curve (nAUC), fraction of hits found (FH), shortfall (SF), percentage of recovered hits that are DepMap common-essential genes (%ess), and the effective number of Reactome level-2 pathway groups at batch (EP-B), screen (EP-S), and dataset (EP-D) scope. For EP-B/EP-S/EP-D, each gene is assigned to one of its pathway groups at random and each scope is subsampled to a fixed annotated-gene count (30, 200, and 6000, respectively), so the three metrics are not directly comparable across scopes. Random is an instantiation of the random policy, not an expected value. All performance metrics are computed separately for each screen and then averaged equally across the 20 test screens. See full results in Supplementary Table <a href="#A3.T4" title="Supplementary Table 4 ‣ Appendix C Complete Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</span></span></figcaption>
<div id="S2.T1.6" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:198.1pt;vertical-align:-97.9pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-175.1pt,100.5pt) scale(0.5,0.5) ;">
<p id="S2.T1.6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.T1.6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S2.T1.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:695.2pt;height:399.3pt;vertical-align:-197.4pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(0.0pt,0.0pt) scale(1,1) ;">
<span id="S2.T1.6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.T1.6.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text">
