<span id="S2.T1.6.1.1.1.1.1.1.33.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><math id="S2.T1.m213" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.1</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span id="S2.T1.6.1.1.1.1.1.1.33.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><math id="S2.T1.m214" class="ltx_Math" alttext="39.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>39.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">39.2</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span id="S2.T1.6.1.1.1.1.1.1.33.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><math id="S2.T1.m215" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>18.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18.9</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span id="S2.T1.6.1.1.1.1.1.1.33.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><math id="S2.T1.m216" class="ltx_Math" alttext="47.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>47.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">47.0</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span id="S2.T1.6.1.1.1.1.1.1.33.9" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;"><math id="S2.T1.m217" class="ltx_Math" alttext="68.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>68.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">68.3</annotation></semantics></math></span></span>
</span>
</span></span></span>
</span></span></span></p>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> achieves the strongest performance, with both Gemini-3.1-Pro and GPT-5.6 Sol warm starts reaching EF <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math> 5.67, nAUC 21.7%, and recovering approximately 27.7% of hits at  5% effective library coverage.
This exceeds standalone Gemini-3.1-Pro (EF <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.71" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.71</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.71</annotation></semantics></math>) and GPT-5.6 Sol (EF <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.81</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.81</annotation></semantics></math>), as well as <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> alone (EF <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.83" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.83</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.83</annotation></semantics></math>), supporting the complementarity of the LLM warm start and <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> feedback-conditioned policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Analyzing standalone LLM policies, we observe relatively strong performance, led by GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and GLM-5.1. Removing outcome labels consistently reduces performance, indicating that LLMs use experimental feedback to inform subsequent acquisitions. However, the magnitude of the reduction is modest relative to the performance retained without labels, suggesting that their acquisition behavior remains strongly driven by information available before observing assay-specific outcomes. These results help revisit and contextualize previous findings on LLM-driven sequential experimental design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite> (additional details in Appendix <a href="#A11" title="Appendix K Revisiting whether LLMs can learn from lab-in-the-loop feedback ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></a>), while highlighting a limitation of standalone LLM policies that <span id="S2.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> is explicitly designed to overcome.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> achieves considerably higher mean EF than methods that adapt within a screen without leveraging historical screen data, including BioBO, Probability-of-Hit, LLMNN, and ICBR-EF. The comparatively stronger performance of BPMF, Screen-kNN, and MAML, methods not specifically designed for adaptive hit discovery but that leverage available training screens, further underscores the value of transferring knowledge from historical experiments, a central motivation behind the design of <span id="S2.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>A illustrates the complementary strengths of the two components of <span id="S2.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span>. The LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro shown in the figure) performs strongly in the early rounds, where its extensive biological prior gives it an advantage over methods that must learn from iterative feedback, but its performance gradually plateaus. By contrast, <span id="S2.SS3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> relies primarily on experimental feedback: it starts from lower scores, with limited screen-specific information before the first batch, but improves steadily as outcomes accumulate. <span id="S2.SS3.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> combines these strengths, leveraging the LLM to prioritize promising hits in the initial rounds before handing off to the learned policy, which expands discovery by adapting to the accumulating experimental feedback. Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A5.F1" title="Supplementary Figure 1 ‣ E.2 Qualitative analysis of AssayLoop on two biologically distinct screens ‣ Appendix E Example Inputs ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> illustrates the same pattern in more detail for two individual test screens.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having established <span id="S2.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> performance on held-out screens, we next investigated how historical screens contribute to policy learning, how far the learned policy transfers beyond the biology represented in training, and which design choices drive performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, we investigated data-scaling behavior by examining how <span id="S2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> performance varies with the number of available training screens.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>C, mean performance increases across the evaluated training-set sizes, with EF@10 more than doubling over the scaling range and no clear evidence of saturation at the largest dataset size. By contrast, increasing model capacity yields little additional benefit across a nearly 40-fold range in parameter count, indicating that performance in this regime is primarily limited by the number of historical screens rather than model size (Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Model Scaling ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We next evaluated transfer to phenotype categories absent from training using leave-one-phenotype-out (LOPO) models across the five phenotype categories in <span id="S2.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span>, holding out one category for evaluation while training on screens from the remaining four. The amount of data withheld varies substantially across these experiments
(Supplementary Table <a href="#A1.T1" title="Supplementary Table 1 ‣ Appendix A Dataset Composition ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), therefore we interpret LOPO primarily as a test of robustness to phenotype exclusion. Across the full test set, <span id="S2.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> trained under LOPO reaches EF <math id="S2.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.59" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.59</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.59</annotation></semantics></math>, compared with <math id="S2.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.83" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.83</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.83</annotation></semantics></math> under full training, resulting in a smaller mean EF drop than Screen-kNN LOPO (<math id="S2.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.24" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.24</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.24</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="S2.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.42" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.42</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.42</annotation></semantics></math>; Fig. <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>B). Overall, <span id="S2.SS4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> under LOPO remains above other methods trained on all phenotypes, including Screen-kNN (<math id="S2.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.40</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.40</annotation></semantics></math>), MAML (<math id="S2.SS4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.77" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.77</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.77</annotation></semantics></math>), and BPMF (<math id="S2.SS4.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.49" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.49</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.49</annotation></semantics></math>). These results indicate that <span id="S2.SS4.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> performance is not solely dependent on access to training screens from the same phenotype category, supporting its generalization to unseen phenotype categories.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.SS4.fig1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/Figure4_Results_revised.svg" id="S2.SS4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/319;" width="476" height="319"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.SS4.fig1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Figure: 4: <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop<span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> outperforms existing methods at adaptive hit discovery and improves
with historical experience.</span></span> All panels report performance on the 20 temporally held-out test
screens of <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> (<math id="S2.SS4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=10</annotation></semantics></math> rounds of <math id="S2.SS4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b=100</annotation></semantics></math> genes).
<span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>, Fraction of all screen hits recovered as a function of the effective fraction of the
library acquired, averaged over test screens. <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> recovers hits fastest throughout the
campaign. Gemini 3.1 Pro is competitive over the first rounds, reflecting a strong biological prior,
but its trajectory flattens as observations accumulate, whereas <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> hands off to <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> and continues to gain.
<span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">B</span>, Phenotype-held-out transfer. EF for <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> and Screen-kNN trained on the
full training set, and in a leave-one-phenotype-out (LOPO) regime in which every training screen
belonging to the evaluated phenotype category is removed. Screen-kNN degrades sharply under LOPO,
while <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> is largely preserved and, under LOPO, still exceeds Screen-kNN trained on all
phenotypes.
<span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">C</span>, Data scaling. 216 <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> models were trained on nested subsets of 1 to 1,349
training screens (more models were trained in the low-data regime to reduce noise). Left, EF at acquisition step <math id="S2.SS4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>; right, the acquisition budget (as a percentage of
the library) required to reach a given recall of the screen hits. Solid lines, supervised
fine-tuning; dashed lines, after GRPO fine-tuning; shading, the gain attributable to RL. Performance
increases monotonically with the number of training screens, with no clear plateau over the evaluated range. For this scaling analysis, we omit the screen-description input to isolate scaling trends of the in-context (i.e., history-conditioned) capabilities.
<span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">D</span>, Gene token initialization. EF after SFT (light) and after RL fine-tuning (dark)
for gene embeddings initialized at random, from GenePT, from K562 expression, and from three
factorizations of the training hit matrix (SVD, MF, BPMF). Initializations that encode cross-screen
hit structure substantially outperform embeddings derived from external biological data.
<span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">E</span>, <span id="S2.SS4.fig1.1.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> ablations. Removing the screen description <math id="S2.SS4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> from the input, or
replacing the context-delta reward with EF directly, both reduce EF.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we performed multiple ablations to identify important architectural choices (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>D-E, full ablations in Supplementary Table <a href="#A2.T3" title="Supplementary Table 3 ‣ B.2 Training strategies ‣ Appendix B Ablations ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Two design choices contributed meaningfully to performance and offered additional insight into how the policy operates. The first aspect is gene token initialization: in our experiments, embeddings derived from the training hit matrix (BPMF, SVD, MF) outperform those derived from external biological data, such as GenePT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> or K562 essential-gene Perturb-seq experiments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, with BPMF resulting in the best performance after RL fine-tuning (EF <math id="S2.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.83" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.83</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.83</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S2.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.40</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.40</annotation></semantics></math> for SVD; Fig. <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>D). The second aspect is that policy training benefits from <em id="S2.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">both</em> conditioning on the assay and explicitly rewarding the policy for exploiting that context: either removing the screen description <math id="S2.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> or replacing the context-delta reward (which explicitly encourages leveraging the context) with terminal EF degrades performance (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>E). While conditioning on the screen description generally improves model performance, we also notice that <span id="S2.SS4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span>’s handoff design provides a broader mechanism for incorporating screen-specific contextual knowledge through the LLM in the early rounds, which leads to a substantial boost in performance (Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.3 AssayLoop improves adaptive hit discovery on held-out screens ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para"><img src="2609.11877v1/Figure5_Biodiversity_revised.png" id="S2.SS4.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/429;" width="476" height="429" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Figure 5: <span id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop<span id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> acquires biologically diverse perturbations and encodes directional
gene-gene relationships.</span></span>
<span id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>, Reactome pathway composition of the genes acquired by six representative methods,
pooled over the 20 test screens (1,000 acquisitions per screen). Inner ring, the eight largest
top-level Reactome categories, with all remaining roots pooled into <em id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Other</em>; outer ring,
second-tier groups within each category, shown as tints of the parent hue. <em id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Random</em> is the
composition of the annotated gene universe, i.e. the expected composition of a uniformly drawn
batch (EP metrics are calculated for the expected distribution). The number at the centre is the dataset-level effective number of pathway groups (EP-D), values below each ring give the corresponding
batch-level (EP-B) and screen-level (EP-S) quantities. Screen-kNN is the most concentrated
repertoire (EP-D <math id="S2.SS4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="54.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>54.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">54.8</annotation></semantics></math>), over-weighting RNA metabolism; Gemini-3.1-Pro retains
broad dataset-level breadth (EP-D <math id="S2.SS4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="66.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>66.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">66.2</annotation></semantics></math>) but has lower diversity within individual batches (EP-B <math id="S2.SS4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>14.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14.5</annotation></semantics></math>); <span id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> combines high dataset-level diversity (EP-D <math id="S2.SS4.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="70.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>70.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70.4</annotation></semantics></math>) with broad batch
coverage (EP-B <math id="S2.SS4.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>18.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18.4</annotation></semantics></math>).
<span id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">B</span>, Directional gene-gene influence learned by <span id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>. Influence is defined as
the change in the acquisition score of a target gene when a probe gene is added to the observed
history as a hit, relative to a background context of 50 randomly drawn genes, averaged over 10
independently sampled backgrounds. Influence patterns are calculated under a fixed, generic screen description to inspect model-wide influence patterns learned by the model. Left, influence matrix for a panel of 31 genes comprising 12
canonical cancer drivers (upper-left block) and 19 genes from functional modules; rows are probe
genes and columns are target genes. The matrix is markedly
asymmetric, showing that the model encodes directional updates rather than gene
similarity. Right, the highest-magnitude probe<math id="S2.SS4.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>target pairs remaining after removal of pairs annotated in databases (Methods).
<span id="S2.SS4.p6.1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">C</span>, Context-dependent influences with literature-supported biological connections. Bars compare the influence of each probe–target pair in the indicated focal screen with its mean influence across the other 19 held-out screens, holding all other inputs fixed. Both genes are true hits in the focal screen, and the pair is absent from databases. Cartoons summarize literature-supported shared biological contexts involving HUSH recruitment, translational stress sensing, and TFIIIC/INO80 activity at tRNA genes.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.5 </span><span id="S2.SS5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> preserves biological breadth while enriching for hits</h3>

<div id="S2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond hit discovery performance, we examined the biological diversity of acquired perturbations using the effective number of Reactome pathway groups (EP) at three scopes: within a batch (EP-B), within a screen (EP-S), and across the full test dataset (EP-D).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.3 AssayLoop improves adaptive hit discovery on held-out screens ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>A, standalone LLMs show lower diversity within batches and screens (EP-B <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="13" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>13</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S2.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math>, EP-S <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S2.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="35" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>35</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35</annotation></semantics></math>), but substantially broader coverage across the full dataset. For example, Gemini-3.1-Pro reaches EP-D <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="66.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>66.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">66.2</annotation></semantics></math>, close to BPMF (<math id="S2.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="72.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>72.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">72.5</annotation></semantics></math>) and BioBO (<math id="S2.SS5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="72.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>72.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">72.6</annotation></semantics></math>). In contrast, it achieves a proportionally much lower within-screen diversity (EP-S <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="34.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>34.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">34.6</annotation></semantics></math>) compared to those two methods (<math id="S2.SS5.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50.7</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50.6</annotation></semantics></math>). Such behavior is consistent with LLMs focusing on different screen-specific biological programs across assays, while exploring a narrower biological neighborhood within each individual screen. Such focused prioritization is well suited to providing an initial warm start, but may limit exploration over multiple acquisition rounds.
Further, we find that methods that do not leverage training screens, such as BioBO and Probability-of-Hit, maintain high diversity within screens and across the dataset, consistent with broader exploration rather than concentration on historically frequent hits.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> similarly explores more broadly within individual batches and screens (EP-B <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="19.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>19.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">19.3</annotation></semantics></math>; EP-S <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="46.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>46.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">46.7</annotation></semantics></math>), while maintaining high dataset-level diversity (EP-D <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>65.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65.0</annotation></semantics></math>). <span id="S2.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> retains comparable breadth while improving hit-discovery performance: with Gemini-3.1-Pro, it achieves similar or higher batch-, screen and dataset-level diversity (EP-B <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>18.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18.4</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="19.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>19.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">19.3</annotation></semantics></math>; EP-S <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="46.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>46.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">46.6</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="46.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>46.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">46.7</annotation></semantics></math>; EP-D <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="70.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>70.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70.4</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S2.SS5.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>65.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65.0</annotation></semantics></math>), while increasing EF from 4.83 to 5.67. Thus, <span id="S2.SS5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> combines the focused early prioritization of the LLM with <span id="S2.SS5.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> biological breadth across the screen, while achieving higher hit enrichment than either component alone.
Additional per-model diversity analysis, including pathway composition across LLM families, is provided in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Biological Diversity Analysis ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.6 </span><span id="S2.SS6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> encodes directional gene–gene influence patterns</h3>

<div id="S2.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Because <span id="S2.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> updates its acquisition scores as observations accumulate, we can ask how observing one gene as a hit changes the prioritization of others. We define the
<em id="S2.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">influence</em> of a probe (that is, observed) gene on a target gene as the change in the target gene’s acquisition score when the probe is added to an otherwise matched history as a hit, measured
against a background context of 50 randomly drawn genes and averaged over 10
independently sampled contexts (Methods). The influence therefore captures a directional update encoded by the learned acquisition policy, rather than a calibrated interaction probability or evidence of causality. Nonetheless, these learned dependencies provide a way to interrogate the biological structure underlying the learned policy and to nominate gene relationships for further investigation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, we probed model-wide influence patterns under a fixed generic screen description, averaging over randomized background histories (Methods). Figure <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>B (left) shows the influence matrix for a panel of 31
genes: 12 canonical cancer drivers and 19 genes drawn from functional modules. Within this panel, the learned relationships are asymmetric: <math id="S2.SS6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="44\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>44</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">44\%</annotation></semantics></math> of reciprocal pairs have influences of
opposite sign. For example, adding MDM2 to the history as a hit increases the predicted score of
PFDN4 by <math id="S2.SS6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.33" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.33</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.33</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas adding PFDN4 decreases the predicted score of MDM2 by
<math id="S2.SS6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.46" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.46</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.46</annotation></semantics></math>. These asymmetric relationships cannot be explained by a purely symmetric gene-similarity representation: observing one gene can change the prioritization of another in a direction that is not reciprocated.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To ask whether these learned relationships extend beyond established annotations, we removed pairs represented in STRING, CORUM, SIGNOR, MSigDB, or
Reactome <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> and examined the highest-magnitude remaining influences
(Fig. <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>B, right).
Among the positive pairs, including MYC in the hit history increases the score of SMU1 and PRPF4. These learned associations are consistent with established links between oncogenic MYC and dependence on spliceosome machinery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>.
Similarly, MDM2 increases the prioritization of EMG1 and PNO1, two factors essential for small-subunit ribosome biogenesis. Biologically, disrupting ribosome biogenesis stabilizes p53 via the RPL5/RPL11-5S-RNP-MDM2 nucleolar surveillance pathway <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>.
Supporting a functional connection, PNO1 depletion has been shown to increase RPL11–MDM2 association and stabilize p53 in TP53-wild-type colorectal cancer cells <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>.
Among negative influences, several high-magnitude pairs have plausible pathway-level precedent but lack direct experimental validation. For example, SMAD4 decreases the prioritization of NDUFS7 and NFU1, consistent with reported links between SMAD4 loss and altered mitochondrial respiration in pancreatic cancer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>.
Similarly, the NRAS-to-AMOTL2 influence is consistent with indirect pathway-level evidence: although oncogenic NRAS activates Hippo signaling in melanocytes, and parallel BRAF-driven MAPK activation reduces expression of the YAP/TAZ target AMOTL2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>, AMOTL2 was not directly evaluated under NRAS mutation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Because <span id="S2.SS6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> conditions jointly on the screen description and observed history, we next explore whether learned influences vary across assay contexts. We search for pairs with substantially stronger influence in one held-out screen than across the remaining 19, requiring both genes to be hits in the focal screen and excluding pairs annotated in databases (Methods). For input context, we use the first 100 genes suggested by the LLM (Gemini-3.1), following the <span id="S2.SS6.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> protocol, and hit labels assigned from the ground truth data. This exploratory analysis identified three examples with literature-supported pathway-level connections (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>C): DCAF1→ZNF638, IGHMBP2→GCN1, and GTF3C1→ACTR5. In each case, influence is substantially larger in the focal screen than across other test contexts. These examples illustrate context dependence in the learned policy and nominate hypotheses for follow-up, rather than establishing direct genetic interactions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.7 </span>Post-training LLMs can improve sequential hit discovery</h3>

<figure id="S2.SS7.fig1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/Figure6_AssayLLM_revised.svg" id="S2.SS7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/240;" width="476" height="240"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.SS7.fig1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Figure 6:
<span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Post-training improves sequential hit-discovery performance in an open-weight LLM.</span>
<span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>, <span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span> training pipeline. Acquisition trajectories are first collected by running GLM-5.1 as an acquisition policy over the <span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> training screens. A 27B-parameter Qwen3.6 backbone is then supervised fine-tuned (SFT) on these trajectories, exposing it to the sequential acquisition protocol and experimental feedback while training it to emit parseable gene batches. Two variants are optimized with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO): a standalone policy
trained on full <math id="S2.SS7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>-round rollouts (3A), and a warm-start policy trained on the handoff campaign, in
which <span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span> controls the first <math id="S2.SS7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=3</annotation></semantics></math> rounds before the frozen <span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> completes the
remaining rounds (3B).
<span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">B</span>, Enrichment factor (EF) on the 20 test screens for the Qwen 3.6 27B base model, after SFT
on GLM-5.1 traces, and after SFT+GRPO (<span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span>), each acting as a standalone policy; and for the
two <span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> configurations in which <span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span> provides the warm start before handing off to
<span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>. Post-training raises standalone EF by 39% over the base model, and the
handoff-trained variant approaches the GLM-5.1<math id="S2.SS7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S2.SS7.fig1.1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> configuration.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our preceding results show that historical experiments can be used to learn a feedback-conditioned acquisition policy that generalizes to held-out screens, and that this capability complements the biological knowledge encoded in pretrained LLMs. We therefore asked whether adaptive acquisition behavior could be learned directly within an LLM through task-specific post-training, thereby directly integrating learned experimental decision-making with pretrained biological knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As a proof of concept, we introduce <span id="S2.SS7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span>, a domain-specific LLM acquisition policy built on the 27B-parameter Qwen 3.6 backbone. <span id="S2.SS7.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span> is trained in two stages (Fig. <a href="#S2.SS7" title="2.7 Post-training LLMs can improve sequential hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.7</span></a>A): supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on complete acquisition trajectories generated by a stronger teacher model (GLM-5.1), followed by group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to directly optimize screen-level hit discovery, with rollouts from the same
screen forming a group to control for screen difficulty (Methods).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Post-training substantially improves performance on <span id="S2.SS7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> (Fig.  <a href="#S2.SS7" title="2.7 Post-training LLMs can improve sequential hit discovery ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.7</span></a>B; Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.3 AssayLoop improves adaptive hit discovery on held-out screens ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Starting from Qwen3.6-27B, SFT increases EF from 2.65 to 3.56, and subsequent GRPO further increases EF to 3.69, corresponding to a 39% improvement over the base model. <span id="S2.SS7.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span> approaches its larger GLM-5.1 teacher (EF 4.0), showing that a substantial fraction of the teacher’s acquisition performance can be transferred to a smaller open-weight model. The post-training improvement from EF 2.65 to 3.69 substantially narrows the gap to <span id="S2.SS7.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> (4.83). These gains, combined with the strong zero-shot acquisition performance of frontier LLMs (Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.3 AssayLoop improves adaptive hit discovery on held-out screens ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), motivate extending the same strategy to stronger pretrained LLMs as a path toward more capable standalone adaptive policies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We further asked whether post-training could optimize an LLM specifically for its role as the warm-start policy in <span id="S2.SS7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span>. We therefore trained a second <span id="S2.SS7.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span> variant in the handoff setting, in which the LLM controls the first <math id="S2.SS7.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> rounds before handing the accumulated context to <span id="S2.SS7.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> (Methods). In this setting, the objective rewards not only overall hit discovery but also the quality of the experimental history constructed for <span id="S2.SS7.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> (Methods). Using <span id="S2.SS7.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span> as the warm-start policy yields an EF of <math id="S2.SS7.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.05</annotation></semantics></math>, while handoff-aligned training further increases EF to <math id="S2.SS7.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.23" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.23</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.23</annotation></semantics></math>, approaching the GLM-5.1 <math id="S2.SS7.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S2.SS7.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> configuration (EF <math id="S2.SS7.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.27" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.27</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.27</annotation></semantics></math>). Together, these results provide a proof of principle that historical screens and simulated trajectories can be used to post-train LLMs both as standalone adaptive policies and to better complement a specialized feedback-conditioned acquisition model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span>, a comprehensive benchmark for adaptive hit discovery in CRISPR screens, spanning 1,389 screens across five phenotype categories with dedicated metrics that account for incomplete libraries and LLM-specific failure modes. By providing standardized evaluation at a scale two orders of magnitude larger than previous benchmarks, <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> enables both rigorous comparison of acquisition strategies and, crucially, the training of policies that transfer across experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Building on this resource, <span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> achieves the strongest performance among the methods evaluated, recovering an average 27.7% of hits while assaying 5% of the candidate library.
The handoff design, in which an LLM provides biologically informed prioritization in early rounds before transitioning to <span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> for feedback-conditioned adaptation, outperforms both components used in isolation, supporting the complementarity of these two capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our results clarify the role of LLMs in adaptive experimental design. While we confirm that frontier LLMs do incorporate experimental feedback to some degree, their in-context adaptation remains limited compared to a policy explicitly trained for this purpose.
This finding, consistent across multiple families, suggests that current general-purpose LLMs are particularly effective as sources of biological prior knowledge, while policies explicitly trained for feedback-conditioned adaptation make more effective use of accumulating experimental outcomes.
Domain-specific post-training, as demonstrated by <span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span>, can substantially narrow this gap and improve adaptive acquisition behavior directly within an LLM: trajectory-level supervision and deployment-aligned reinforcement learning yield a 39% improvement over the base model, and handoff-aligned training further improves its performance as the warm-start policy in <span id="S3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The data scaling analysis shows that <span id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> performance improves consistently with the number of available training screens, with no clear plateau over the range evaluated. Combined with the strong leave-one-phenotype-out generalization results, this suggests that larger and more diverse screen collections may further improve transferable acquisition policies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Several limitations define the scope of this study. <span id="S3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> is a retrospective benchmark focused on genome-wide screens with sufficient hit signal, and the policies evaluated here remain to be validated prospectively in a live experimental loop. We also focus on binary hit discovery under a fixed acquisition budget; extending the framework to richer readouts and heterogeneous experimental costs will be important directions for future work. Finally, the retrospective formulation treats observed screen outcomes as fixed labels and does not explicitly model experimental noise across replicates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Because <span id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> represents each experimental task through a natural-language description, the same benchmark formulation can in principle extend beyond the phenotypes and modalities currently represented to encompass diverse perturbation experiments and richer biological readouts. <span id="S3.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLLM</span> represents a particularly promising avenue in this direction: as an LLM-based policy, it can flexibly represent new experimental readouts, perturbation types, and biological contexts through its text interface, while its post-training strategy provides a mechanism for incorporating new screening data as it becomes available. More broadly, the iterative, lab-in-the-loop paradigm explored here motivates a future in which adaptive experimental design and biological foundation model training are coupled, with each experimental campaign both advancing biological discovery and generating data that improves the models guiding subsequent experiments.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
