<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Qualitative analysis of <span id="A5.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> on two biologically distinct screens</h3>

<figure id="A5.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/paper_handoff_composition_pathway.svg" id="A5.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/396;" width="476" height="396"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="A5.F1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Qualitative Analysis of <span id="A5.F1.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> on two biologically distinct screens.<span id="A5.F1.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We show the composition of genes of suggested acquisition rounds across three models: <span id="A5.F1.8.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> (top row), Gemini-3.1-Pro (bottom row), and the <span id="A5.F1.8.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span> handoff from Gemini (middle row). On the left side of the figure, we have a <math id="A5.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{NF-}\kappa\text{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>NF-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>B</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{NF-}\kappa\text{B}</annotation></semantics></math> / TNF signaling screen. On the right side, we have a AAV transgene silencing screen. For each subplot (representing a screen-model pair), we have two histograms. The upper histogram shows the proposed acquisition batch at each acquisition round. The lower histogram shows the composition of hits from that batch. For example, in the AAV screen, <span id="A5.F1.8.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> proposes 100 genes for the first batch, with DNA repair being the largest category. The bars are colored according to gene pathways from Reactome. </span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Gene Embedding Analysis</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix provides additional analysis of the gene embeddings used
by <span id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>, complementing the ablation in
Section <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Embedding initialization ‣ Appendix B Ablations ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Embedding drift during training</h3>

<div id="A6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A natural question is whether <span id="A6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> reshapes the gene embedding
geometry during training or preserves the structure imposed by the
initialization. We examine this for all ablated embedding types by
measuring two complementary quantities: pairwise cosine similarity
preservation and gene-neighborhood stability.</p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pairwise cosine similarity.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each embedding type, we
compute the pairwise cosine similarity between 300,000 randomly sampled
gene pairs before and after training. As reported in the main text
(Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A6.F2" title="Supplementary Figure 2 ‣ Gene-neighborhood stability. ‣ F.1 Embedding drift during training ‣ Appendix F Gene Embedding Analysis ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), BPMF embeddings are almost perfectly
preserved (Pearson <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.999" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.999</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.999</annotation></semantics></math>). This indicates that the geometry
provided by BPMF is already well-suited for the acquisition task and
that <span id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> learns its policy on top of this fixed structure
rather than reorganizing it.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Gene-neighborhood stability.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further quantify structural
changes using rank-biased overlap
(RBO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite> between the 100 nearest neighbors of
each gene before and after each training stage. For BPMF, the median RBO
between initialization and the final RL model exceeds <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.95</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.95</annotation></semantics></math>, confirming
that gene neighborhoods are largely unchanged.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A6.F2" title="Supplementary Figure 2 ‣ Gene-neighborhood stability. ‣ F.1 Embedding drift during training ‣ Appendix F Gene Embedding Analysis ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the degree of embedding
drift across all ablated embedding types. The drift varies
dramatically across sources. Random embeddings undergo near-complete
reorganization during supervised fine-tuning, as expected. Other
matrix-factorization variants (SVD, MF, MF-Sphere) also show
substantial neighborhood changes during supervised fine-tuning, though
less than random initialization. Interestingly, GenePT embeddings show
relatively little drift despite their poor downstream performance,
suggesting that embedding stability alone does not explain the advantage
of BPMF. In all cases, the RL fine-tuning stage produces much smaller
changes than supervised fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these results suggest that the effectiveness of BPMF stems not
merely from stability but from providing a geometry that is both stable
<em id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">and</em> well-aligned with the adaptive hit-discovery objective.
Other embeddings are either reshaped during training (random, SVD, MF)
without converging to an equally effective geometry, or are stable but
encode structure less relevant to the task (GenePT).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/gene_embedding_drift_by_source.svg" id="A6.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:324/619;" width="324" height="619"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="A6.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Embedding drift during training for all ablated embedding types.<span id="A6.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The effect of training on embedding geometry differs dramatically by embedding type. BPMF embeddings show near-perfect preservation of gene neighborhoods, while other initializations undergo substantial reorganization during supervised fine-tuning.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Embedding initialization and biological plausibility</h3>

<figure id="A6.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/gene_embedding_init_story.svg" id="A6.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/298;" width="381" height="298"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="A6.F3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Recovering textbook biology does not predict task usefulness.<span id="A6.F3.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We take initial embeddings and measure how much they recover gene-gene relationships from four well known databases: STRING, CORUM, SIGNOR, and REACTOME. We compute gene-gene similarity scores with cosine similarity. Ground truth labels are assigned to be 1 if the relationship exists in the database, otherwise 0. AUROC is calculated using these scores and then averaged across the four databases. Interestingly, we find that embeddings which capture these databases most closely (e.g., GenePT, K562 embeddings) are more difficult to train <span id="A6.F3.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> on, whereas methods which initialize directly from historical screen data (matrix factorization approaches) are most useful. </span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As discussed in Section <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Embedding initialization ‣ Appendix B Ablations ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>, we observe a negative
association between how well an embedding source recovers canonical
biological relationships and its downstream performance as an
<span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> initialization. Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A6.F3" title="Supplementary Figure 3 ‣ F.2 Embedding initialization and biological plausibility ‣ Appendix F Gene Embedding Analysis ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> visualizes
this relationship. For each embedding type, we compute pairwise
cosine similarity between genes and measure the AUROC for recovering
known gene-gene relationships from STRING <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>,
CORUM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, SIGNOR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, and
Reactome <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, averaged across the four
databases. GenePT and K562 embeddings, which capture these known
relationships best, provide the weakest initialization for <span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>.
Conversely, matrix-factorization approaches that learn directly from
historical screen data perform best, despite encoding less canonical
biology. This suggests that the gene-gene structure most relevant to
adaptive hit discovery is not well captured by established pathway and
interaction databases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Structure of the BPMF embedding space</h3>

<figure id="A6.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.11877v1/paper_bpmf_k10_organization_hdbscan.png" id="A6.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:452/505;" width="452" height="505" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F4.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="A6.F4.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">BPMF embeddings organize by screen phenotype, rather than physical complex or pathway.<span id="A6.F4.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Embeddings are <math id="A6.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=10</annotation></semantics></math> dimensions and are visualized with PCA (left) and cosine UMAP (right). </span>Top: HDBSCAN<span id="A6.F4.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. Genes are clustered in the original space with HDBSCAN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite> with minimum cluster size 150, each labeled by its dominant phenotype association. Note that several clusters are associated with DNA-damage response without further disambiguation. </span>Middle: CORUM Complexes<span id="A6.F4.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. The embeddings are colored by CORUM complexes grouped into general families (top 10 groups, grey = other). This coloring shows minimal grouping across the space. </span>Bottom: Reactome pathways.<span id="A6.F4.8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The largest 10 Reactome pathways are used to color the embeddings, similarly revealing a lack of distinct spatial clustering except in the common essential gene area.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand why BPMF embeddings are effective, we visualize and
cluster the <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{g}=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{g}=10</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional embedding space. Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A6.F4" title="Supplementary Figure 4 ‣ F.3 Structure of the BPMF embedding space ‣ Appendix F Gene Embedding Analysis ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>
shows PCA and cosine-UMAP projections of the BPMF gene embeddings,
colored by three different annotation schemes.</p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">HDBSCAN clustering.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We cluster genes in the original
embedding space using HDBSCAN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite> with a minimum cluster
size of 150. The resulting clusters align primarily with screen
phenotype categories rather than molecular pathway or complex
membership. We identify clusters corresponding to common essential,
context-essential, and selectively essential genes, as well as clusters
associated with immune response and apoptosis. Notably, five distinct
clusters are associated with the DNA-damage response, which we were
unable to further disambiguate into more specific phenotypes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Canonical annotations.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also color the embeddings by CORUM
protein complexes and Reactome pathways, each grouped into high-level
families. In both cases, the coloring reveals minimal spatial clustering:
genes belonging to the same complex or pathway are distributed across
the embedding space rather than forming compact groups. The exception is
the common-essential gene region, which shows partial organization by
Reactome pathway membership.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Interpretation.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These observations indicate that the BPMF
embedding space is organized primarily by shared screen phenotype —
reflecting how genes co-occur as hits across historical CRISPR screens
— rather than by canonical pathway or complex membership. This is
consistent with the finding in Section <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Embedding initialization ‣ Appendix B Ablations ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a> that
embeddings which better recover canonical biological relationships
(STRING, CORUM, SIGNOR, Reactome) provide weaker initialization for
<span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>. The BPMF embeddings capture a distinct, phenotype-derived
representation of gene function, in which proximity reflects shared
perturbation profiles across screens rather than established biological
annotations. Their strong performance suggests that these
phenotype-derived embeddings may complement existing gene embedding
approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> and motivates their evaluation in
other downstream tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Biological Diversity Analysis</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A7.F5" title="Supplementary Figure 5 ‣ Appendix G Biological Diversity Analysis ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> breaks down the Reactome composition of acquired genes by individual LLM, complementing the method-level comparison in Figure <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Adaptive experimental capability scales with historical experience and transfers across phenotype categories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>A.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.11877v1/llm_pathway_heatmap.png" id="A7.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/313;" width="476" height="313" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A7.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="A7.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">LLMs converge to similar distributions of biology across families.<span id="A7.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The heatmap shows top-level composition of requested genes in terms of Reactome pathways, aggregated across the 20 test screens. Unique genes is the total number of distinct genes requested across all tested screens. Annotated picks is the percent of requested genes which have ground truth labels. The Random baseline is the pathway distribution given by uniform sampling over the universe of all possible genes. Cells are colored by by the ratio between the observed pathway share for that model and the expected share size of Random, where red = over-represented and blue = under-represented (color values capped between 0.5x and 2x). Overall, LLMs generally show similar gene acquisition signatures, with an emphasis on RNA and protein metabolism and under-representation of bulk metabolism and developmental biology. While there are differences between models, they are small compared to the difference from other baseline methodologies such as kNN. Additionally, the number of effective pathways for each LLM falls into a narrow range. Note that Kimi-K2.6 and Opus tend to supply less than the requested number of genes (100) in many cases, possibly due to biological safety training, resulting in a low number of unique genes. </span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Metrics used in <span id="A8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span></h2>

<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Below we define the metrics used in <span id="A8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> to evaluate the performance of hit discovery models.
We let <math id="A8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the set of all possible genes, <math id="A8.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> the set of genes in the gene library of a given screen (the set of genes for which a label <math id="A8.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> is available), <math id="A8.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> the set of hits in <math id="A8.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A8.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> the set of genes acquired by the model over the <math id="A8.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rounds.
Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A8.F6" title="Supplementary Figure 6 ‣ Appendix H Metrics used in AssayBench-Loop ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> provides a visual overview of the metrics and their definitions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/assayloop-ef-metrics-v15.svg" id="A8.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/297;" width="476" height="297"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A8.F6.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A8.F6.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Example of Enrichment Factor and other metrics<span id="A8.F6.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. </span>A)<span id="A8.F6.11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The definition of our adjusted enrichment factor (EF). </span>B)<span id="A8.F6.11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Terms used for normalizing budget calculations. </span>C)<span id="A8.F6.11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> A worked example of EF showing how EF is comparable across screens. Note, no adjustment for untested genes is needed in this computation. </span>D)<span id="A8.F6.11.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Example of hit recovery trajectories from real baselines. </span>E)<span id="A8.F6.11.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The definition used to calculate adjusted normalized AUC (nAUC). </span>F)<span id="A8.F6.11.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Additional metrics used for understanding model behavior.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hit enrichment factor (EF)</h5>

<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our main metric is the hit enrichment factor (EF), that measures the ratio between the number of hits found and the expected number of hits found by random selection.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We write <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{L}=|G_{T}\cap L|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{L}=|G_{T}\cap L|</annotation></semantics></math> the number of acquired genes over the full trajectory present in the screen library, <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\mathcal{G}}=|G_{T}\cap\mathcal{G}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\mathcal{G}}=|G_{T}\cap\mathcal{G}|</annotation></semantics></math> the number of valid acquired genes, <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}}}=|G_{T}\setminus\mathcal{G}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∖</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}}}=|G_{T}\setminus\mathcal{G}|</annotation></semantics></math> the number of hallucinated acquired genes that do not represent valid genes, and <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\mathrm{miss}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>miss</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\mathrm{miss}}</annotation></semantics></math> for the total
number of unfilled acquisition slots over the <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rounds. Finally, <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\text{rand}}=|H|/|L|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mtext>rand</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\text{rand}}=|H|/|L|</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the random hit rate. We define the hit enrichment factor as</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A8.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A8.E19"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A8.E19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{EF}=\frac{|G_{T}\cap H|}{(N_{L}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}}}+N_{\text{miss}})\cdot h_{\text{rand}}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>EF</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>miss</mtext></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mtext>rand</mtext></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{EF}=\frac{|G_{T}\cap H|}{(N_{L}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}}}+N_{\text{miss}})\cdot h_{\text{rand}}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(19)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This formula differs from the classical enrichment factor (<em id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">i.e.,</em> <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{|G_{T}\cap H|}{|G_{T}|\cdot h_{\text{rand}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mtext>rand</mtext></msub></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{|G_{T}\cap H|}{|G_{T}|\cdot h_{\text{rand}}}</annotation></semantics></math>) in the number of acquired genes that are used for the normalization. By normalizing with <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(N_{L}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}}}+N_{\text{miss}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>miss</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(N_{L}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}}}+N_{\text{miss}})</annotation></semantics></math>, we do not penalize acquisition of real genes (<math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g\in\mathcal{G})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g\in\mathcal{G})</annotation></semantics></math> that are not part of the screen library but do penalize the acquisition of hallucinated genes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Normalized area under the cumulative-hits curve (nAUC)</h5>

<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also report the normalized area under the cumulative-hits curve (nAUC), which captures the full acquisition trajectory rather than only the endpoint. We construct the curve by plotting the fraction of hits found against the fraction of the library effectively queried, with one point per acquisition batch. For each batch <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1,\ldots,T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1,\ldots,T</annotation></semantics></math>, we denote <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{L,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{L,t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}},t}</annotation></semantics></math> for the cumulative number of in-library and hallucinated acquired genes in <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> respectively, and <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{H,t}=|G_{t}\cap H|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{H,t}=|G_{t}\cap H|</annotation></semantics></math> for the number of hits in <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Unlike in
Eq.<a href="#A8.E19" title="In Hit enrichment factor (EF) ‣ Appendix H Metrics used in AssayBench-Loop ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>, unfilled acquisition slots do not advance <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, so an under-supplying
policy ends its curve at a smaller <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> rather than being carried flat to the full budget. This keeps nAUC a measure of ordering quality. The cumulative-hits curve is then composed of points with coordinates <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\big(\frac{1}{|L|}(N_{L,t}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}},t}),\frac{1}{|H|}N_{H,t}\big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\big(\frac{1}{|L|}(N_{L,t}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}},t}),\frac{1}{|H|}N_{H,t}\big)</annotation></semantics></math> for each batch.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The area under this piecewise-linear curve is computed by trapezoidal integration and normalized by the AUC of a perfect oracle that ranks all hits before any non-hit, over the same effective budget. The perfect oracle AUC is computed over a curve with coordinates <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\big(x_{t},min(x_{t}\cdot|L|/|H|,1)\big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\big(x_{t},min(x_{t}\cdot|L|/|H|,1)\big)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are the coordinates of the predictor curve (<math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}=\frac{1}{|L|}(N_{L,t}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}},t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}=\frac{1}{|L|}(N_{L,t}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}},t})</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A8.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A8.E20"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A8.E20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{nAUC}=\frac{\text{AUC}}{\text{AUC}_{\text{oracle}}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>nAUC</mtext><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mtext>AUC</mtext><msub><mtext>AUC</mtext><mtext>oracle</mtext></msub></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{nAUC}=\frac{\text{AUC}}{\text{AUC}_{\text{oracle}}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(20)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AUC}_{\text{oracle}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>AUC</mtext><mtext>oracle</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AUC}_{\text{oracle}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the area under the optimal curve evaluated at <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=(N_{L}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}}})/|L|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=(N_{L}+N_{\bar{\mathcal{G}}})/|L|</annotation></semantics></math>. A value of <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math> indicates the model acquires all hits in the screen first. Random acquisition yields <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{nAUC}\approx|H|/|L|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>nAUC</mtext><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{nAUC}\approx|H|/|L|</annotation></semantics></math> (the hit rate) in expectation when <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|G_{T}|&lt;|H|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|G_{T}|&lt;|H|</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fraction of hits (FH)</h5>

<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the fraction of hits found over the whole trajectory, measuring the recall of the acquisition policy. Using the same notation, this is defined as</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A8.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A8.E21"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A8.E21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{FH}=\frac{|G_{T}\cap H|}{|H|}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>FH</mtext><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{FH}=\frac{|G_{T}\cap H|}{|H|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(21)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">i.e. the number of hits acquired by the model divided by the total number of hits in the screen. Only in-library genes can be hits, so out-of-library and hallucinated acquisitions do not contribute to the numerator. A value of <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math> means all hits in the screen were found within the acquisition budget.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Shortfall (SF)</h5>

<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the shortfall as the fraction of acquired genes that fall outside the screen’s gene library. Using the same notation:</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A8.EGx8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A8.E22"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A8.E22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{SF}=\frac{|G_{T}\setminus L|}{|G_{T}|}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>SF</mtext><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∖</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{SF}=\frac{|G_{T}\setminus L|}{|G_{T}|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(22)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">i.e. the number of acquired genes not present in the screen library divided by the total number of acquisitions. This includes both real genes outside the library (<math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{T}\cap(\mathcal{G}\setminus L)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>∖</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{T}\cap(\mathcal{G}\setminus L)</annotation></semantics></math>) and hallucinated genes (<math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{T}\setminus\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∖</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{T}\setminus\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Percentage of essential genes (<math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\%_{\text{ess}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>%</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>ess</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%_{\text{ess}}</annotation></semantics></math>)</h5>

<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some genes are hits in a given screen just because these genes typically lead to cell death in general, also known as essential genes. While these genes are genuine hits, they do not always reflect the particularities of the biology studied in the screen. We report their fraction among recovered hits as a diagnostic of how strongly acquisition is concentrated on broadly essential genes.
We used the list of 1,827 common essential genes from the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> denote the set of common essential genes, the percentage of essential genes is simply</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A8.EGx9" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A8.E23"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A8.E23.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\%_{\text{ess}}=\frac{|G_{T}\cap H\cap E|}{|G_{T}\cap H|}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>%</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>ess</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\%_{\text{ess}}=\frac{|G_{T}\cap H\cap E|}{|G_{T}\cap H|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(23)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">i.e. the number of acquired hits that are common essentials divided by the total number of acquired hits.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effective Pathways (EP)</h5>

<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We quantify the biological breadth of acquired genes using the effective number of Reactome level-2 pathway groups (186 groups in total). This is calculated using the first order Hill number</p>
<table id="A8.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A8.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="EP=\exp(H(p))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">EP=\exp(H(p))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> is Shannon entropy and <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is the distribution of pathways in the sample set (assuming they were sampled uniformly).</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To make methods with different acquisition and annotation rates comparable, we rarefy each scope to a fixed number of annotated genes: <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=30</annotation></semantics></math> per batch (EP-B), <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=200</annotation></semantics></math> per screen (EP-S), and <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=6000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=6000</annotation></semantics></math> across the complete test set (EP-D). Sample sets containing fewer than the required number of annotated genes are excluded. We average over 400 Monte Carlo draws for EP-B and EP-S and 300 draws for EP-D. EP-B is averaged within each screen and then across screens, whereas EP-S is averaged directly across screens.
Because a gene may be annotated to multiple groups, in each Monte Carlo draw we assign every annotated gene to exactly one of its associated groups.
Assigning one group per gene prevents heavily annotated genes from artificially increasing diversity.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, EP is expressed as an effective number of equally represented pathway groups, with larger values indicating broader biological coverage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Batch diversity metrics: Vendi score (VS) and Pathway overlap (PO)</h5>

<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report two complementary diversity metrics for the acquired batches, measuring whether the model selects functionally diverse genes or concentrates on a narrow biological neighborhood at each step.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vendi Ratio (VR).</span> For each batch, we compute gene embeddings using GenePT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, construct the cosine-similarity Gram matrix <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> of all acquired genes in the batch <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and compute its Vendi score <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, which corresponds to the effective number of distinct genes in <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (1 means all embeddings of genes in <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are collinear and <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|B_{t}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|B_{t}|</annotation></semantics></math> means all embeddings are orthogonal). We report the Vendi ratio, which is normalized by <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|B_{t}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|B_{t}|</annotation></semantics></math> and averaged across batches. A higher Vendi ratio means the genes acquired in the batch are more diverse.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pathway overlap (PO).</span> For each batch, we compute the mean pairwise Jaccard overlap of GO biological-process annotations between the acquired genes, and divide it by the same quantity for a batch of equal size drawn uniformly at random from the screen library. Averaging across batches gives PO. A value of <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.00</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.00</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to random selection, values above <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> indicate that acquired genes share more annotations than expected by chance (a narrow biological neighborhood), and values below <math id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> indicate a broader batch. PO and VS are complementary: VR measures diversity in a continuous embedding space, whereas PO measures it through discrete pathway membership.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A9" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix I </span><span id="A9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> Reveals Directional Gene-Gene Relationships</h2>

<figure id="A9.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.11877v1/gene_matrix_featured_heatmap.png" id="A9.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:419/364;" width="419" height="364" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F7.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A9.F7.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Influence heatmap showing how discovered hits affect predictions.<span id="A9.F7.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Given a probe gene (rows) and target gene (columns), we measure the change in the acquisition score of the target gene from <span id="A9.F7.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> when the probe gene is reported as a hit in context. The first 12 genes are important canonical cancer drivers (oncogenes and tumor suppressors). The next 19 are representative functional-module genes. </span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Because <span id="A9.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> updates its predictions as experimental
observations accumulate, we can probe the learned policy to ask how
observing one gene as a hit changes its predictions for other genes. For
a probe-target pair, we construct a random background context of 50
genes, measure the acquisition score of the target, and then measure it
again after adding the probe gene to the context as a hit. We define the
difference between these predictions as the <em id="A9.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">influence</em> of the
probe on the target, and average this quantity across 10 independently
sampled background contexts. So we can inspect model-wide influence patterns learned by the model, we use a generic screen description “A genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to identify essential genes”.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A9.F7" title="Supplementary Figure 7 ‣ Appendix I AssayFormer Reveals Directional Gene-Gene Relationships ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows the resulting influence matrix for 31
representative genes, including 12 canonical cancer drivers and 19 genes
from functional modules. Influences among cancer drivers are relatively
weak, consistent with these genes acting through distinct biological
programs. In contrast, substantially stronger influences emerge among
functionally related gene pairs,
indicating that <span id="A9.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> has learned structured, context-dependent
relationships from historical screens.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, these relationships are strongly directional rather than
simple symmetric associations. The correlation between the influence
matrix and its transpose is only <math id="A9.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.16</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A9.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="44\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>44</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">44\%</annotation></semantics></math> of reciprocal
gene pairs have influences with opposite signs. For example, observing
MDM2 as a hit increases the acquisition score of PFDN4 by <math id="A9.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.33" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.33</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.33</annotation></semantics></math>,
whereas observing PFDN4 as a hit decreases the acquisition score of MDM2
by <math id="A9.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.46" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.46</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.46</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, the model does not simply encode gene similarity:
observing a gene can induce a directional update in the predicted
relevance of another gene, and the effect need not be reciprocal.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To test whether this procedure can uncover meaningful relationships
beyond canonical annotations, we remove gene pairs represented in the
STRING, CORUM, SIGNOR, MSigDB, and Reactome databases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> and examine
high-magnitude remaining influences, shown in
Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A9.F8" title="Supplementary Figure 8 ‣ Appendix I AssayFormer Reveals Directional Gene-Gene Relationships ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. Among positively influenced pairs, we
identify relationships consistent with co-essentiality or
synthetic-lethal dependencies, such as increased spliceosome dependence
following MYC hits and increased nucleolar-stress dependence following
MDM2 hits. Conversely, negative influences highlight patterns consistent
with epistatic masking or lineage-specific exclusion, including reduced
dependence on mitotic machinery following PIK3CA hits and reduced OXPHOS
dependence following SMAD4 hits.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A9.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/paper_influence_figure.svg" id="A9.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/225;" width="476" height="225"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F8.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A9.F8.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="A9.F8.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gene influence scores reveal hidden epistatic relationships not captured by standard interaction databases.</span>
For each probe gene (left of arrow), we measure the change in the model’s predicted influence score for every target gene (right of arrow) when the probe gene is observed as a hit, averaged over random background contexts. <span id="A9.F8.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left:</span> Boosted pairs. <span id="A9.F8.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right:</span> Suppressed pairs. These dependencies describe the model’s inferred decision process rather than established biological interactions.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A10" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix J </span>Model Scaling</h2>

<div id="A10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate whether performance gains similar to those from additional training data can be obtained by increasing model capacity. We train 150 models spanning a nearly 40-fold range in parameter count, from 0.28M (XS) to 10.97M (XL), including our default 4.44M-parameter model (L). In contrast to data scaling, we observe no meaningful improvement with increasing model size (Supplementary Fig. <a href="#A10.F9" title="Supplementary Figure 9 ‣ Appendix J Model Scaling ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>). This suggests that, in the current data regime, available training screens rather than model capacity are the binding constraint on performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A10.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/scaling_combined_lines.svg" id="A10.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/361;" width="476" height="361"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A10.F9.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A10.F9.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance scales with data, but not model size.<span id="A10.F9.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <span id="A10.F9.10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> models (without input screen descriptions) are trained to identify scaling of in-context learning capabilities. </span>Top:<span id="A10.F9.10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Models are trained on varying amounts of data from 1 to all training screens, and average performance curves are plotted. Both SFT and RL show this performance increase, with RL boosting SFT performance. </span>Top Left plot<span id="A10.F9.10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> is EF at <math id="A10.F9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> acquisition steps, and shows that scaling is most effective during the first few steps of the experiment. At 100 steps (10,000) genes sampled, models approach similar performance. This is expected because even a random model will find all hits if it samples the entire genome. </span>Top Right plot<span id="A10.F9.10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> is budget to acquire enough hits to satisfy a recall threshold <math id="A10.F9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, to find <math id="A10.F9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=50\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the hits, the ‘1349’ model requires sampling less than 30% of the full genome. Note that RL rollouts stop at 10 steps during training, so these curves reflect out-of-distribution gains for RL performance. </span>Bottom:<span id="A10.F9.10.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We also consider scaling model size from XS (0.28M parameters) to XL (10.97M parameters), given the full training set. Here, we do not observe meaningful scaling laws. We posit that larger training datasets are required to show evidence of model scaling. Note that scaling models has shown useful performance gains in pretrained LLMs on the non-active learning setting of AssayBench (Figure 4 from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A11" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix K </span>Revisiting whether LLMs can learn from lab-in-the-loop feedback</h2>

<div id="A11.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work has investigated whether LLMs can serve directly as
acquisition policies in lab-in-the-loop biological experiments.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gupta et al. [17]</a></cite> found that the performance of several LLM-based
experimental-design agents was largely insensitive to feedback provided
during the experiment, whereas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wainrib et al. [51]</a></cite> showed that
sufficiently capable LLMs can benefit substantially from experimental
feedback. We revisit this question on <span id="A11.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayBench-Loop</span> by evaluating a range
of LLMs with and without access to the outcome labels from previous
acquisition rounds. Unlike these prior studies, which randomized hit
assignments in their control conditions, we simply omit the hit labels
while preserving the history of previously acquired genes. This provides
a direct measure of how much each model benefits from observing
experimental outcomes. We additionally compare to <span id="A11.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> without context; in this setting, we simply take the top 1,000 genes predicted by <span id="A11.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> with no context.</p>
</div>
<div id="A11.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Supplementary Figure <a href="#A11.F10" title="Supplementary Figure 10 ‣ Appendix K Revisiting whether LLMs can learn from lab-in-the-loop feedback ‣ Biology-in-the-loop:Amortized Adaptive Hit Discovery in CRISPR Screens" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, removing hit labels consistently
reduces performance across all tested LLMs, demonstrating that these
models do use experimental feedback to adapt their subsequent
acquisitions. This result is consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wainrib et al. [51]</a></cite> and
confirms that adaptive in-context learning extends across multiple LLM
families. However, the magnitude of this adaptation remains limited:
standalone LLMs are consistently outperformed by <span id="A11.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>, which shows a substantially larger gain from feedback. Furthermore, <span id="A11.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayLoop</span>, which
utilizes an LLM for early acquisitions and delegates later acquisition rounds to <span id="A11.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span>, shows both strong label-blind performance and also shows better in-context learning than LLMs. Thus, while current frontier LLMs can learn from experimental outcomes in context, a policy explicitly trained for feedback-conditioned adaptation remains more
effective for sequential hit discovery.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A11.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.11877v1/llm_label_ablation.svg" id="A11.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:310/276;" width="310" height="276"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A11.F10.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="A11.F10.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">LLM performance with and without per-round hit labels<span id="A11.F10.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. We tested the in-context learning capabilities of select LLMs by running the active learning framework <span id="A11.F10.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">without</span> labels from previous rounds of experiments. This allows us to distinguish between the ability of LLMs to incorporate experimental feedback with ICL, versus their warm-start capabilities without feedback. Across model families, we found that experimental feedback boosts model performance, indicating that LLMs do benefit from the active learning setting of this task. We also show the performance of <span id="A11.F10.7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AssayFormer</span> with and without context, illustrating its relatively poor ability without feedback but substantially stronger ICL capabilities.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</article>
